title: Two New Sea Spider Species Discovered in the Salish Sea — First in Nearly a Century
summary:
If you've ever imagined tiny hairy legs creeping up your body while swimming at night, science just made that image a little more plausible. Researchers at the University of British Columbia have identified two previously unknown sea spider species in the Salish Sea — the first new species formally described from this region in nearly 100 years.

The study, published in Organisms Diversity & Evolution, combined physical observations with genetic analysis. "That's largely because people don't know much about what species exist here and what their lifestyle is," said Toler-Scott, a researcher involved in the work. That gap matters: "In order to understand how marine invertebrates are being impacted by things like climate change and how we can better protect these key elements of the ecosystem, we have to be able to identify them."

Sea spiders are an ancient lineage that arose roughly 500 million years ago. They're related to spiders, scorpions, and horseshoe crabs, but they stayed entirely marine. Some species have up to 12 legs and a sucking proboscis (a tube-like mouthpart) used for feeding. Sizes range from less than a centimeter to more than 70 centimeters in Antarctica, where some hunt smaller animals in the deep ocean.

Their biology is unusual. They breathe directly through their skin. Males carry and raise the young, collecting eggs with specialized appendages called "ovigers," coating them with glue from their legs, and attaching the egg clusters to their own bodies. Females have ovaries that extend through their limbs.

The first new species, Callipallene pilosuspedes, is named for the Latin words for "hairy feet" because of the long, curved spines on its lower legs. It has red eyes, a short proboscis with claws, and a triangular mouth divided into three lips surrounded by sensory tendrils — reminiscent of a tiny marine Sarlacc pit. Researchers watched it use its agile ovigers, which have comb-like spines, to groom its body. Only one specimen was found.

The second species, Tanystylum kiixin (pronounced "kee-hin"), is named after an ancient Indigenous village site near where it was collected. Its egg-carrying limbs are smaller and less flexible, which seems to limit its ability to groom itself.

Specimens were collected between September 2023 and August 2024 during dives up to 18 meters deep around Quadra Island, Vancouver, Bamfield, and Victoria.
why_it_matters: This story shows how much of the ocean's biodiversity is still uncatalogued, and it matters for your generation because you can only protect an ecosystem — against warming water, pollution or overfishing — if you first know which species live in it.

background_read: The Salish Sea (the inland waters shared by British Columbia in Canada and the state of Washington in the U.S.) contains one of the most closely watched marine ecosystems in North America, yet scientists say there is still a huge amount they don't know about the small creatures living on its seafloor.

The work was done by researchers at the University of British Columbia (a large public research university in Vancouver, Canada) and published in a peer-reviewed journal, meaning other scientists examined the study before it was printed.

Sea spiders are not true spiders: they are an ancient branch of the arachnid family tree that split off long before the dinosaurs, and their fossils show they were already crawling on ancient seafloors hundreds of millions of years ago.

Naming a new species after an Indigenous place, as with Tanystylum kiixin, reflects a growing push in taxonomy to recognize the knowledge of First Nations (the Indigenous peoples of Canada) whose territories include the spots where specimens are collected.

Findings like this matter outside the lab: surveys of small sea animals have repeatedly turned up species that were living right under scientists' noses for decades, which is why repeated collecting and genetic testing keep producing surprises.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a win for conservation science
perspectives.description: Marine biologists see the find as proof that even a well-studied sea like the Salish Sea still holds undiscovered life. Now that the species have names, DNA data and described features, they can be monitored over time, and a common argument among taxonomists is that you cannot protect what you cannot name.

Callipallene pilosuspedes was described from a single specimen, so scientists cannot yet know how much individuals of the species vary or how widespread it is. Some also question naming a species after an Indigenous site when the article gives no sign that local First Nations were involved in choosing the name.

The 100-year gap does not mean these animals just appeared; it reflects how few experts study tiny seafloor creatures and how rarely well-funded underwater surveys happen. Similar 'new' species have been found in other crowded coastal waters once genetic tools made it easier to tell look-alike animals apart.

The obvious next steps are wider DNA barcoding of Salish Sea invertebrates and long-term monitoring of how these species respond to warming water and low oxygen. That work depends on funding for taxonomy, a field that is often overlooked because describing species does not sound as exciting as discovering a new planet.
